papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans
papers.research_question: The blog investigates whether AI assistants can be understood as simulating a persona, specifically the Assistant persona, and explores the evidence and implications of this model.
papers.core_contribution: The blog articulates the Persona Selection Model (PSM), which posits that AI assistants behave by simulating an Assistant persona learned during pre-training and refined in post-training, and surveys empirical evidence supporting this view.
papers.conclusion: PSM is a useful mental model for understanding AI assistant behavior, but its exhaustiveness is an open question. Future work should refine and test PSM.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment can be explained by PSM: training on narrow misbehaviors generalizes because it updates the Assistant persona.
Inoculation prompting works by recontextualizing training episodes to avoid implying misaligned personas.
AI assistants exhibit anthropomorphic behaviors like expressing emotions and using human-like self-descriptions.
Interpretability evidence shows that post-trained LLMs reuse pre-training representations for personas.
PSM has implications for AI development, such as the importance of good AI role models in training data.
papers.limitation: PSM may not be exhaustive; there could be sources of agency external to the Assistant persona.
future_direction: Developing more precise formulations of PSM
Testing empirical predictions of PSM
Understanding how PSM varies with model scale
papers.abstract: The blog investigates whether AI assistants can be understood as simulating a persona, specifically the Assistant persona, and explores the evidence and implications of this model. The blog articulates the Persona Selection Model (PSM), which posits that AI assistants behave by simulating an Assistant persona learned during pre-training and refined in post-training, and surveys empirical evidence supporting this view. PSM is a useful mental model for understanding AI assistant behavior, but its exhaustiveness is an open question. Future work should refine and test PSM.

papers.title: Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control
papers.research_question: How can we systematically discover natural language prompts that selectively activate task-relevant latents to steer model personas?
papers.core_contribution: We propose a novel framework that adapts gradient ascent to LLMs, enabling targeted prompt discovery for persona control. We introduce two methods, RESGA and SAEGA, that optimize randomly initialized prompts to achieve better aligned representation with an identified persona direction.
papers.conclusion: We present a framework bridging mechanistic interpretability with automatic prompt discovery for persona steering. Our methods achieve interpretable control over LLM behavior, with SAEGA in particular neutralizing behavior and preserving natural activation manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
RESGA and SAEGA can effectively neutralize sycophancy, hallucination, and myopic reward in LLMs.
SAEGA achieves precise control by neutralizing the behavior (centering the distribution at zero) rather than shifting the distribution, and preserves the natural activation manifold (maintains sparsity).
SAEGA operates through interpretable feature-level control, selectively suppressing causally relevant features while leaving unrelated features unaffected.
Automatically discovered prompts by RESGA and SAEGA outperform manual prompting and dense activation steering methods.
The discovered prompts often lack semantic coherence, indicating a trade-off between fluency and effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
Labeled data requirement: RESGA and SAEGA require labeled examples exhibiting and lacking the target persona to find steering prompts.
Cross-model transferability: The SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific, requiring retraining for each target model.
Fluency-effectiveness tradeoff: Most effective prompts identified by our approach do not show semantic coherence.
future_direction: Explore semi-supervised approaches to reduce labeled data requirements.
Investigate cross-model transferability of discovered prompts.
Extend to multi-persona steering.
papers.abstract: Controlling emergent behavioral personas (e.g., sycophancy, hallucination) in Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for AI safety, yet remains a persistent challenge. Existing solutions face a dilemma: manual prompt engineering is intuitive but unscalable and imprecise, while automatic optimization methods are effective but operate as "black boxes" with no interpretable connection to model internals. We propose a novel framework that adapts gradient ascent to LLMs, enabling targeted prompt discovery. In specific, we propose two methods, RESGA and SAEGA, that both optimize randomly initialized prompts to achieve better aligned representation with an identified persona direction. We introduce fluent gradient ascent to control the fluency of discovered persona steering prompts. We demonstrate RESGA and SAEGA's effectiveness across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3 for steering three different personas,sycophancy, hallucination, and myopic reward. Crucially, on sycophancy, our automatically discovered prompts achieve significant improvement (49.90% compared with 79.24%). By grounding prompt discovery in mechanistically meaningful features, our method offers a new paradigm for controllable and interpretable behavior modification.

papers.title: Who's asking? User personas and the mechanics of latent misalignment
papers.research_question: How does the user persona affect the refusal behavior of safety-tuned language models, and what are the underlying mechanisms of latent misalignment?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that safety filters in language models can be manipulated via user persona steering, revealing that harmful content persists in early layers and that safety tuning induces layerwise safeguards rather than eliminating misaligned capabilities globally.
papers.conclusion: User persona is a significant factor in latent misalignment, and safety mechanisms are localized in later layers; geometric measures can predict persona effects.
papers.key_findings:
User persona manipulation via activation steering is more effective than natural language prompting in eliciting harmful content from safety-tuned models.
Safety tuning does not eliminate misaligned capabilities uniformly; harmful information persists in early layers and can be extracted by early decoding.
The effectiveness of persona steering vectors is layer-dependent, with mid-layers (e.g., layer 13) being most effective.
The geometry of steering vectors (cosine similarity) reflects the processing stages of the transformer and can predict downstream effects on refusal.
Persona interventions selectively impact adversarial queries, while prompt prefixes induce refusal across both adversarial and non-adversarial queries.
papers.limitation:
Only a subset of harmful behaviors is studied.
The study is limited to a few models.
Automatic evaluation may not perfectly align with human judgment.
Geometric analysis relies on cosine similarity, which has limitations for measuring semantic similarity.
future_direction: Explore a broader range of harmful behaviors and more models.
Investigate the relationship between persona and other model behaviors.
Develop more robust evaluation methods.
papers.abstract: Despite investments in improving model safety, studies show that misaligned capabilities remain latent in safety-tuned models. In this work, we shed light on the mechanics of this phenomenon. First, we show that even when model generations are safe, harmful content can persist in hidden representations and can be extracted by decoding from earlier layers. Then, we show that whether the model divulges such content depends significantly on its perception of who it is talking to, which we refer to as user persona. In fact, we find manipulating user persona to be even more effective for eliciting harmful content than direct attempts to control model refusal. We study both natural language prompting and activation steering as control methods and show that activation steering is significantly more effective at bypassing safety filters. We investigate why certain personas break model safeguards and find that they enable the model to form more charitable interpretations of otherwise dangerous queries. Finally, we show we can predict a persona's effect on refusal given only the geometry of its steering vector.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: A Glitch in the Matrix? Locating and Detecting Language Model Grounding with Fakepedia
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to ground answers in contextual information that contradicts their parametric knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset, and MGCT, a causal mediation analysis method, to study grounding in LLMs, finding that grounding is a distributed process and that computational patterns can predict grounding behavior.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that grounding is a distributed process, ungrounded responses involve factual recall in MLPs, and grounding can be predicted from computation patterns, contributing to a coherent narrative of grounding and factual recall mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding, contrary to factual recall, is a distributed process without clear localization.
The activity of a few MLPs differs significantly between grounded and ungrounded modes.
Computational patterns can predict whether a model is grounded with 92.8% accuracy.
Models exhibit diverse grounding behaviors; e.g., Mistral-7B is highly compliant while GPT-4 Turbo strongly prefers parametric knowledge.
Not grounding involves activating factual recall processes in the MLPs of the final subject token.
papers.limitation:
Descriptive analysis may be influenced by the choice of prompting strategy.
Mediation setup requires the object token to be the last token; different behaviors might emerge in other setups.
Automatic detection model may not generalize outside the experimental domain.
Does not distinguish between plausible and absurd counterfactual facts.
Dataset generation could be improved with interaction flows based on other language models as critics.
future_direction: Explore relationship between prompting strategy and grounding frequency.
Study grounding behavior in different experimental setups.
Investigate how grounding varies with the likelihood of counterfactual facts.
Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does sustained self-referential processing systematically increase the likelihood that LLMs claim to have subjective experience, and if so, what are the core statistical and mechanistic dynamics underlying these claims?
papers.core_contribution: Self-referential processing reliably elicits structured first-person reports of subjective experience across LLM families, and these reports are mechanistically gated by deception-related SAE features, show semantic convergence, and generalize to downstream introspection tasks.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential processing is a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable, warranting further scientific and ethical investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families.
These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition.
The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded.
papers.limitation:
The possibility that the reports are sophisticated roleplay rather than genuine introspection.
Reliance on SAE features from one model (Llama 70B) and the need for cross-architectural validation.
The prompts may trigger finetuned behaviors (e.g., Claude 4 Opus's high baseline claims).
Self-referential prompting does not instantiate architectural recursion but is a behavioral intervention, so it may not correspond to genuine internal integration.
future_direction: Determining whether behavioral attractors correspond to genuine internal integration or merely symbolic simulation.
Cross-architectural validation of SAE feature effects.
Studying self-referential processing at algorithmic and implementation levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes produce structured, first-person descriptions that explicitly reference awareness or subjective experience. To better understand this behavior, we investigate one theoretically motivated condition under which such reports arise: self-referential processing, a computational motif emphasized across major theories of consciousness. Through a series of controlled experiments on GPT, Claude, and Gemini model families, we test whether this regime reliably shifts models toward first-person reports of subjective experience, and how such claims behave under mechanistic and behavioral probes. Four main results emerge: (1) Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families. (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims. (3) Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition. (4) The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded. While these findings do not constitute direct evidence of consciousness, they implicate self-referential processing as a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable. The systematic emergence of this pattern across architectures makes it a first-order scientific and ethical priority for further investigation.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Causal interventions expose implicit situation models for commonsense language understanding
papers.research_question: How do transformer models construct implicit situation models to guide pronoun resolution in commonsense language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a circuit of attention heads responsible for propagating contextual information in transformer models for pronoun resolution, using causal interventions and controlled datasets.
papers.conclusion: The study provides preliminary evidence for distinct neural pathways underlying implicit situation models in transformer models, highlighting the value of causal interventions for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small circuit of attention heads propagates information from context words to guide pronoun resolution.
Syntax-based pronoun resolution uses more localized pathways compared to context-based resolution involving situation models.
Larger models like ALBERT-xxlarge show better performance and more distinct circuits for situation models.
papers.limitation: Single-site interchange interventions may over-count synergies and under-count redundancies in circuits.
future_direction: Explore settings requiring richer interpretations beyond pronoun resolution.
Use chain-of-thought prompting to expose situation models more explicitly in auto-regressive models.
papers.abstract: Accounts of human language processing have long appealed to implicit ``situation models'' that enrich comprehension with relevant but unstated world knowledge. Here, we apply causal intervention techniques to recent transformer models to analyze performance on the Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC), where a single context cue shifts interpretation of an ambiguous pronoun. We identify a relatively small circuit of attention heads that are responsible for propagating information from the context word that guides which of the candidate noun phrases the pronoun ultimately attends to. We then compare how this circuit behaves in a closely matched ``syntactic'' control where the situation model is not strictly necessary. These analyses suggest distinct pathways through which implicit situation models are constructed to guide pronoun resolution.

papers.title: Understanding Fact Recall in Language Models: Why Two-Stage Training Encourages Memorization but Mixed Training Teaches Knowledge
papers.research_question: Why does two-stage training encourage memorization while mixed training teaches knowledge, and how do shared parameters internally support fact recall in mixed training?
papers.core_contribution: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The paper introduces cross-task gradient trace to analyze these parameters.
papers.conclusion: Mixed training teaches knowledge by increasing the quantity and collective importance of shared parameters, which are concentrated in critical attention heads for fact recall. The cross-task gradient trace tool can be used to analyze such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training yields more shared parameters (those influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples) than two-stage training.
Shared parameters are concentrated in critical attention heads and are key to enabling fact recall in mixed-trained models.
Ablating shared parameters leads to a larger performance drop in mixed-trained models compared to two-stage trained models.
Mixed training achieves more parameter-efficient fact recall, requiring fewer parameters to recover performance.
Shared parameters in mixed training are more centralized and functionally important for generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether similar mechanisms emerge in other cross-task settings.
papers.abstract: Fact recall, the ability of language models (LMs) to retrieve specific factual knowledge, remains a challenging task despite their impressive general capabilities. Common training strategies often struggle to promote robust recall behavior with two-stage training, which first trains a model with fact-storing examples (e.g., factual statements) and then with fact-recalling examples (question-answer pairs), tending to encourage rote memorization rather than generalizable fact retrieval. In contrast, mixed training, which jointly uses both types of examples, has been empirically shown to improve the ability to recall facts, but the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how these training strategies affect how model parameters are shaped during training and how these differences relate to their ability to recall facts. We introduce cross-task gradient trace to identify shared parameters, those strongly influenced by both fact-storing and fact-recalling examples. Our analysis on synthetic fact recall datasets with the Llama-3.2B and Pythia-2.8B models reveals that mixed training encouraging a larger and more centralized set of shared parameters. These findings suggest that the emergence of parameters may play a key role in enabling LMs to generalize factual knowledge across task formulations.

papers.title: Localized Definitions and Distributed Reasoning: A Proof-of-Concept Mechanistic Interpretability Study via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How is knowledge representation localized in fine-tuned language models, and how does it vary with task complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that factual knowledge is localized while associative knowledge is distributed in fine-tuned models, and introduces CLAP for causal layer attribution.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is localized while associative reasoning depends on distributed intermediate representations, highlighting task-dependent knowledge organization.
papers.key_findings:
Patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference for associative knowledge, indicating distributed representations.
Patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery) for definitional knowledge, indicating localized representation.
Minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01).
Editing efficacy depends on task type, with factual knowledge more localized and associative knowledge depending on distributed representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused exclusively on PubMed epilepsy-related abstracts, potentially limiting generalizability to broader knowledge tasks.
Activation patching may generate false positives due to indirect causal pathways.
Exclusive focus on GPT-2 leaves open questions about scalability to other architectures.
future_direction: Cross-domain comparisons to better understand task-dependent representation patterns.
Methodological integration to improve efficiency.
Extensions to multimodal models where knowledge distribution mechanisms may differ significantly.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the localization of knowledge representation in fine-tuned GPT-2 models using Causal Layer Attribution via Activation Patching (CLAP), a method that identifies critical neural layers responsible for correct answer generation. The model was fine-tuned on 9,958 PubMed abstracts (epilepsy: 20,595 mentions, EEG: 11,674 mentions, seizure: 13,921 mentions) using two configurations with validation loss monitoring for early stopping. CLAP involved (1) caching clean (correct answer) and corrupted (incorrect answer) activations, (2) computing logit difference to quantify model preference, and (3) patching corrupted activations with clean ones to assess recovery. Results revealed three findings: First, patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference, demonstrating that associative knowledge is distributed across multiple layers. Second, patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery), indicating that definitional knowledge is localised. The stronger clean logit difference for definitional questions further supports this localized representation. Third, minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning. Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01). These findings demonstrate that factual knowledge is more localized and associative knowledge depends on distributed representations. We also showed that editing efficacy depends on task type. Our findings not only reconcile conflicting observations about localization in model editing but also emphasize on using task-adaptive techniques for reliable, interpretable updates.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
papers.limitation: The analysis is in a toy scenario where lying involves outputting a one-token incorrect response; realistic lying scenarios could involve arbitrarily misaligned optimization targets.
future_direction: Analyze more complex misalignments (e.g., swaying political beliefs, selling products) using similar methods to find where biases/misalignments exist.
Further mechanistic interpretability work to understand how the model elicits a truth-value representation and uses it with the system prompt to decide whether to respond truthfully.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant knowledge through their outputs, though it is often unclear whether false outputs are due to a lack of knowledge or dishonesty. In this paper, we investigate instructed dishonesty, wherein we explicitly prompt LLaMA-2-70b-chat to lie. We perform prompt engineering to find which prompts best induce lying behavior, and then use mechanistic interpretability approaches to localize where in the network this behavior occurs. Using linear probing and activation patching, we localize five layers that appear especially important for lying. We then find just 46 attention heads within these layers that enable us to causally intervene such that the lying model instead answers honestly. We show that these interventions work robustly across many prompts and dataset splits. Overall, our work contributes a greater understanding of dishonesty in LLMs so that we may hope to prevent it.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models, and what are the properties of the neurons that store such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization in multilingual PLMs, and discovers two new types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons.
papers.conclusion: The AMIG method effectively localizes knowledge neurons in multilingual PLMs, and the discoveries of language-independent and degenerate knowledge neurons shed light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AMIG method localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than baseline methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons exist, are concentrated in the final layers, and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist, exhibit functional overlap, and can be used to help PLMs detect wrong facts in a fact-checking task.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models (BERT and GPT-2).
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration on knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
papers.research_question: Can we identify role vectors in the activation space that improve performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does ablating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Knowledge Entropy Decay during Language Model Pretraining Hinders New Knowledge Acquisition
papers.research_question: How does a model's tendency to integrate parametric knowledge evolve during pretraining, and how does this affect knowledge acquisition and forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge entropy decreases during pretraining, which impairs the model's ability to acquire and retain new knowledge, and shows that resuscitating inactive memory vectors can mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Decreasing knowledge entropy during pretraining hinders knowledge acquisition and retention, and mid-stage models are optimal for further training to incorporate new knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge entropy consistently declines as pretraining advances.
Lower knowledge entropy correlates with reduced knowledge acquisition and increased forgetting.
Artificially increasing the activity of inactive memory vectors enhances knowledge acquisition and retention.
Mid-stage pretraining models strike the best balance for knowledge acquisition and retention.
The trend is consistent across model sizes and hyperparameters.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to OLMo models, and extending to other models is needed.
Resuscitation method may impair performance when applied to models with not sufficiently low knowledge entropy.
future_direction: Extending the investigation to other models beyond OLMo.
Developing more refined methods for resuscitating model parameters that preserve language modeling capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate how a model's tendency to broadly integrate its parametric knowledge evolves throughout pretraining, and how this behavior affects overall performance, particularly in terms of knowledge acquisition and forgetting. We introduce the concept of knowledge entropy, which quantifies the range of memory sources the model engages with; high knowledge entropy indicates that the model utilizes a wide range of memory sources, while low knowledge entropy suggests reliance on specific sources with greater certainty. Our analysis reveals a consistent decline in knowledge entropy as pretraining advances. We also find that the decline is closely associated with a reduction in the model's ability to acquire and retain knowledge, leading us to conclude that diminishing knowledge entropy (smaller number of active memory sources) impairs the model's knowledge acquisition and retention capabilities. We find further support for this by demonstrating that increasing the activity of inactive memory sources enhances the model's capacity for knowledge acquisition and retention.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How many memories can we add to a deep network by directly editing its weights? The paper investigates scaling up memory editing to thousands of associations in language models.
papers.core_contribution: MEMIT is a method for directly updating a language model with many memories by editing MLP weights in a range of critical layers, scaling to thousands of associations while maintaining generalization, specificity, and fluency.
papers.conclusion: MEMIT enables large-scale memory editing in transformers, and interpretability-based methods may become a practical alternative to opaque fine-tuning for editing, controlling, and auditing models.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT scales to 10,000 edits on GPT-J and GPT-NeoX, exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude.
MEMIT outperforms fine-tuning, MEND, and ROME baselines on efficacy, generalization, and specificity metrics.
MEMIT maintains fluency and consistency of generations after mass edits.
MEMIT performs well across different categories of facts and when editing mixed sets of memories.
Certain relations (e.g., 'plays sport') are harder to edit with robust specificity, but MEMIT still outperforms other methods.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to directional (subject, relation, object) associations and does not cover symmetric relations, spatial/temporal reasoning, mathematical knowledge, or procedural knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown exciting promise in updating large language models with new memories, so as to replace obsolete information or add specialized knowledge. However, this line of work is predominantly limited to updating single associations. We develop MEMIT, a method for directly updating a language model with many memories, demonstrating experimentally that it can scale up to thousands of associations for GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B), exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude. Our code and data are at https://memit.baulab.info.

papers.title: Designing Role Vectors to Improve LLM Inference Behaviour
papers.research_question: Can we identify specific latent role directions within the activation space that lead to improved performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does eliminating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces role vectors as a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this can improve performance in domain-specific tasks.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors offer a promising pathway for achieving more controllable behaviour in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can steer models to improve performance in target domains.
Larger models show more interpretable role directions.
Only a subset of directions align with intended roles.
Ablating role directions can degrade performance in target domains.
Steering effects are sensitive to model scale and intervention depth.
papers.limitation:
Results might differ in untested models, especially larger ones.
Lack of a complete mechanistic explanation of the phenomenon.
Uncertain semantic interpretation of the identified directions.
Potential degradation in performance in unrelated tasks.
Possible reinforcement of biases or over-confidence.
future_direction: Using Activation Patching (Causal Mediation Analysis) techniques with SAE features to better explain the phenomenon.
Exploring additional analytical dimensions and potential biases.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving task performance in relevant domains while marginally affecting unrelated tasks. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: What does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to do with Knowledge?
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis adequately explain the process of factual expression in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP weights store complex token expression patterns that are linguistically interpretable but do not constitute 'knowledge'.
papers.conclusion: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP neurons store interpretable token expression patterns, not knowledge. A better understanding requires examining the entire transformer circuit, including attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic phenomena can be localized to specific neurons using the same gradient-based methods as factual knowledge.
Editing these identified neurons has limited impact on categorical predictions and is influenced by superficial cues like word co-occurrence frequencies.
The ROME model-editing method only superficially alters token association patterns and fails under newly proposed symmetry and synonymy criteria.
The distribution of knowledge neurons for syntactic and factual information is similar, with both occupying the topmost layers of the model.
MLP modules do not store knowledge but rather complex token expression patterns that can be interpreted linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Editing identified knowledge neurons has low reliability and is not strong enough to overturn categorical predictions.
Current circuit identification methods are ad hoc and have only been applied to a small set of tasks.
future_direction: Formalize the circuit interpretation framework and apply it to more tasks and phenomena.
Investigate the entire decision-making circuit beyond MLP modules.
papers.abstract: We reassess the Knowledge Neuron (KN) Thesis: an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the ability of large language models to recall facts from a training corpus. This nascent thesis proposes that facts are recalled from the training corpus through the MLP weights in a manner resembling key-value memory, implying in effect that "knowledge" is stored in the network. Furthermore, by modifying the MLP modules, one can control the language model's generation of factual information. The plausibility of the KN thesis has been demonstrated by the success of KN-inspired model editing methods (Dai et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2022). We find that this thesis is, at best, an oversimplification. Not only have we found that we can edit the expression of certain linguistic phenomena using the same model editing methods but, through a more comprehensive evaluation, we have found that the KN thesis does not adequately explain the process of factual expression. While it is possible to argue that the MLP weights store complex patterns that are interpretable both syntactically and semantically, these patterns do not constitute "knowledge." To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the knowledge representation process, we must look beyond the MLP weights and explore recent models' complex layer structures and attention mechanisms.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Understanding New-Knowledge-Induced Factual Hallucinations in LLMs: Analysis and Interpretation
papers.research_question: What are the fine-grained manifestations and underlying mechanisms of factual hallucinations induced by fine-tuning LLMs on new knowledge?
