~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers: Addressing Sycophancy in Large Language Models with Pinpoint Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we address sycophancy in Large Language Models by pinpointing and tuning only the components responsible for this behavior, without degrading their general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), a method that identifies a sparse set of attention heads responsible for sycophancy using path patching and then fine-tunes only those heads, effectively mitigating sycophancy while preserving the model's general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Pinpoint tuning is an effective and efficient method to address sycophancy in LLMs by targeting specific internal components, advancing both the understanding and intervention of model behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small percentage (~4%) of attention heads significantly influence sycophantic behavior, as identified by path patching.
Pinpoint tuning these heads effectively reduces sycophancy, outperforming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on sycophancy metrics.
Pinpoint tuning preserves general capabilities (e.g., reasoning, math, code) unlike SFT, which often degrades them.
The method generalizes beyond the training data, as shown on additional sycophancy evaluation datasets.
The identified sycophancy-related heads attend more to tokens that challenge the model compared to other heads.
papers.limitation:
Path patching treats each MLP and attention head as individual nodes, but future work could consider neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for more refined analysis.
The evaluation is based on a specific definition of sycophancy (from Sharma et al. 2023), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other formats of sycophancy.
The verification of pinpoint tuning is mainly conducted on sycophancy; its effectiveness for other abilities requires further investigation.
future_direction: Treating neurons or groups of neurons as atomic units for analysis instead of heads and MLPs.
Investigating generalization to other formats and definitions of sycophancy.
Integrating pinpoint tuning with other interpretability tools like information flow, representation engineering, and sparse auto-encoders.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to prioritize adherence to user prompts over providing veracious responses, leading to the sycophancy issue. When challenged by users, LLMs tend to admit mistakes and provide inaccurate responses even if they initially provided the correct answer. Recent works propose to employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to mitigate the sycophancy issue, while it typically leads to the degeneration of LLMs' general capability. To address the challenge, we propose a novel supervised pinpoint tuning (SPT), where the region-of-interest modules are tuned for a given objective. Specifically, SPT first reveals and verifies a small percentage (<5%) of the basic modules, which significantly affect a particular behavior of LLMs. i.e., sycophancy. Subsequently, SPT merely fine-tunes these identified modules while freezing the rest. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SPT, we conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating that SPT significantly mitigates the sycophancy issue of LLMs (even better than SFT). Moreover, SPT introduces limited or even no side effects on the general capability of LLMs. Our results shed light on how to precisely, effectively, and efficiently explain and improve the targeted ability of LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yellowtownhz/sycophancy-interpretability.

papers.title: ACE: Attribution-Controlled Knowledge Editing for Multi-hop Factual Recall
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing for multi-hop factual recall in LLMs be improved by understanding and leveraging internal neuron-level mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACE, a knowledge editing framework that uses neuron-level attribution to identify and edit query-value pathways, improving multi-hop factual recall.
papers.conclusion: ACE provides a mechanistically grounded solution for multi-hop knowledge editing and establishes a new pathway for advancing KE capabilities based on understanding internal reasoning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs store semantically analogous knowledge in structurally similar transformer components, with query and value neurons for specific knowledge types exhibiting consistent localization patterns.
During multi-hop reasoning, implicit subjects function as query neurons that sequentially activate corresponding value neurons across layers to accumulate information toward the final answer.
ACE outperforms state-of-the-art KE methods by 9.44% on GPT-J and 37.46% on Qwen3-8B in multi-hop accuracy.
Ablating query layers causes a 16.51% performance drop, while omitting value layers leads to a 40.45% decrease, demonstrating the necessity of both components.
GPT-J maintains fixed layer separation for query and value neurons, while Qwen3-8B exhibits dynamic, domain-specific alignment.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on FFN layers and does not edit attention heads, which may limit editability for some knowledge types.
Attribution mechanism relies on first-order Taylor approximation, potentially missing higher-order interactions.
Requires forward passes to compute importance scores, adding computational overhead.
future_direction: Integrating attention head editing into the ACE framework.
Developing more efficient attribution algorithms to reduce computational overhead.
Extending ACE to other model architectures and tasks beyond factual recall.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require efficient knowledge editing (KE) to update factual information, yet existing methods exhibit significant performance decay in multi-hop factual recall. This failure is particularly acute when edits involve intermediate implicit subjects within reasoning chains. Through causal analysis, we reveal that this limitation stems from an oversight of how chained knowledge is dynamically represented and utilized at the neuron level. We discover that during multi hop reasoning, implicit subjects function as query neurons, which sequentially activate corresponding value neurons across transformer layers to accumulate information toward the final answer, a dynamic prior KE work has overlooked. Guided by this insight, we propose ACE: Attribution-Controlled Knowledge Editing for Multi-hop Factual Recall, a framework that leverages neuron-level attribution to identify and edit these critical query-value (Q-V) pathways. ACE provides a mechanistically grounded solution for multi-hop KE, empirically outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 9.44% on GPT-J and 37.46% on Qwen3-8B. Our analysis further reveals more fine-grained activation patterns in Qwen3 and demonstrates that the semantic interpretability of value neurons is orchestrated by query-driven accumulation. These findings establish a new pathway for advancing KE capabilities based on the principled understanding of internal reasoning mechanisms.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often encounter knowledge conflicts when parametric memory contradicts contextual knowledge. Previous works attribute this conflict to the interplay between "memory heads" and "context heads", attention heads assumed to promote either memory or context exclusively. In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. Building upon this insight, we propose Just Run Twice (JuICE), a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric beliefs or contextual knowledge without requiring fine-tuning. JuICE identifies a set of reliable attention heads and leverages a dual-run approach to mitigate the superposition effects. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets and 6 model architectures demonstrate that JuICE sets the new state-of-the-art performance and robust generalization, achieving significant and consistent improvement across different domains under various conflict types. Finally, we theoretically analyze knowledge conflict and the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads, which further elucidates the effectiveness of JuICE in these settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/JUICE.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for final predictions in large language models, specifically for knowledge storage?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static neuron-level attribution method based on log probability increase that outperforms other static methods, and uses it to analyze knowledge storage in attention and FFN layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate 'query neurons', with analysis on six knowledge types helping to understand LLM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed log probability increase method for neuron attribution achieves superior performance compared to seven other static methods across three metrics (MRR, probability, log probability).
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics (e.g., language, country, city) tends to be stored in the same heads, while knowledge with distinct semantics is stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction, despite many neurons contributing.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which in turn are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B; comparing knowledge storage across different models is essential.
Uses static methods for attribution; comparing with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods is important.
future_direction: Explore other types of knowledge beyond the six studied.
Compare knowledge storage similarities and differences across different models.
Compare static attribution methods with other methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs, and what is the functional role of these representations in social reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models develop linearly decodable internal representations of self and others' beliefs in their attention heads, and that manipulating these representations causally alters the model's theory-of-mind performance.
papers.conclusion: Language models develop internal representations of self and others' beliefs that are linearly decodable and play a causal role in social reasoning, suggesting a mechanistic basis for their theory-of-mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can decode the belief status (true/false) of both the protagonist and an omniscient oracle from the activations of specific attention heads in language models.
A subset of attention heads, primarily in middle layers, encodes the belief statuses of both agents independently and in conjunction.
Steering activations along directions that amplify the protagonist's belief and distinguish it from the oracle's belief (+TpFo) significantly improves model performance on false-belief tasks.
The identified belief representations are general and correlated across different social reasoning tasks (Forward Belief, Forward Action, Backward Belief).
Activation interventions along random or single-agent belief directions have minimal impact, highlighting the specificity of the multi-agent belief representation.
papers.abstract: Understanding and attributing mental states, known as Theory of Mind (ToM), emerges as a fundamental capability for human social reasoning. While Large Language Models (LLMs) appear to possess certain ToM abilities, the mechanisms underlying these capabilities remain elusive. In this study, we discover that it is possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents through neural activations of language models, indicating the existence of internal representations of self and others' beliefs. By manipulating these representations, we observe dramatic changes in the models' ToM performance, underscoring their pivotal role in the social reasoning process. Additionally, our findings extend to diverse social reasoning tasks that involve different causal inference patterns, suggesting the potential generalizability of these representations.

papers.title: On Mechanistic Circuits for Extractive Question-Answering
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic circuits be extracted for extractive question-answering, and how can they be used for data attribution and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extracts mechanistic circuits for extractive QA, revealing differences between context and memory faithfulness circuits, and uses insights from the circuits to develop ATTNATTRIB for data attribution and model steering towards context faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that mechanistic circuits for extractive QA can be extracted and used for practical applications like data attribution and model steering, enhancing language model performance and faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct circuits are extracted: a context-faithfulness circuit and a memory-faithfulness circuit.
A small set of attention heads in the context circuit perform reliable data attribution by default.
ATTNATTRIB achieves state-of-the-art attribution results on various extractive QA benchmarks.
Using attributions from ATTNATTRIB can steer the model towards context faithfulness, improving performance by up to 9%.
Circuits for context faithfulness are smaller and involve different components compared to memory circuits.
papers.limitation:
The probe dataset is primarily 0-hop, and ATTNATTRIB performs less well on multi-hop QA.
ATTNATTRIB requires white-box access to the model's parameters, so it cannot be applied to blackbox LLMs.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated strategies that combine ATTNATTRIB with retrieval-based attribution.
Designing a probe dataset consisting of multi-hop questions to improve circuit extraction for multi-hop QA.
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to process documents and facilitate question-answering on them. In our paper, we extract mechanistic circuits for this real-world language modeling task: context-augmented language modeling for extractive question-answering (QA) tasks and understand the potential benefits of circuits towards downstream applications such as data attribution to context information. We extract circuits as a function of internal model components (e.g., attention heads, MLPs) using causal mediation analysis techniques. Leveraging the extracted circuits, we first understand the interplay between the model's usage of parametric memory and retrieved context towards a better mechanistic understanding of context-augmented language models. We then identify a small set of attention heads in our circuit which performs reliable data attribution by default, thereby obtaining attribution for free in just the model's forward pass. Using this insight, we then introduce ATTNATTRIB, a fast data attribution algorithm which obtains state-of-the-art attribution results across various extractive QA benchmarks. Finally, we show the possibility to steer the language model towards answering from the context, instead of the parametric memory by using the attribution from ATTNATTRIB as an additional signal during the forward pass. Beyond mechanistic understanding, our paper provides tangible applications of circuits in the form of reliable data attribution and model steering.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: The Queen of England is not England's Queen: On the Lack of Factual Coherency in PLMs
papers.research_question: What is the coherency of factual knowledge in Pre-trained Language Models, and how does it vary with different prompts and evidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of coherency for factual knowledge in PLMs, demonstrates that PLMs have low coherency, and finds that including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
papers.conclusion: PLMs have poor coherency in factual knowledge, but evidence paragraphs help. Future work should focus on architectural, data, and interface improvements.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs have low coherency in factual knowledge.
Autoregressive PLMs perform worse than masked PLMs.
Optimized prompts do not improve coherency.
Including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
Coherency varies significantly with paraphrased prompts.
papers.limitation: For N-1 or N-M relations, it is difficult to exclude every possible answer, and only answers present in LAMA are excluded, which might negatively affect the results.
future_direction: Improve PLMs on architectural level.
Improve PLMs on data level.
Improve pre-training objectives and interface.
papers.abstract: Factual knowledge encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) enriches their representations and justifies their use as knowledge bases. Previous work has focused on probing PLMs for factual knowledge by measuring how often they can correctly predict an object entity given a subject and a relation, and improving fact retrieval by optimizing the prompts used for querying PLMs. In this work, we consider a complementary aspect, namely the coherency of factual knowledge in PLMs, i.e., how often can PLMs predict the subject entity given its initial prediction of the object entity. This goes beyond evaluating how much PLMs know, and focuses on the internal state of knowledge inside them. Our results indicate that PLMs have low coherency using manually written, optimized and paraphrased prompts, but including an evidence paragraph leads to substantial improvement. This shows that PLMs fail to model inverse relations and need further enhancements to be able to handle retrieving facts from their parameters in a coherent manner, and to be considered as knowledge bases.

papers.title: Identifying and Mitigating Social Bias Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate social biases in language models while preserving individual commonsense knowledge and factual integrity?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a fine-grained debiasing framework (FAST) that localizes and mitigates social bias knowledge in language models while preserving commonsense knowledge, and introduces the BiaScope benchmark for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed fine-grained debiasing framework effectively mitigates social biases while preserving factual knowledge, demonstrating the potential of localized interventions for fairness in language models.
papers.key_findings:
FAST achieves superior debiasing performance on StereoSet, Crows-Pairs, and BiaScope compared to existing methods.
FAST retains commonsense knowledge better than group-invariant debiasing methods, as measured by the Retention Score.
Bias knowledge is localized in specific layers (e.g., the last layer of BERT), and intervening at these layers is most effective.
FAST scales to larger models like GPT2-XL, GPT-Neo-2.7b, and Llama-2-7b, showing consistent debiasing performance.
FAST maintains language modeling capability on downstream GLUE tasks, indicating minimal impact on general performance.
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human-relevant social bias knowledge to process, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive to collect.
Social bias in open language generation or dialogue is not addressed.
Debiasing performance on larger models is less pronounced compared to smaller models.
future_direction: Integrate automated social bias detection methods to enhance construction of biased knowledge base.
Expand the fairness edit method to open language generation or dialogue scenarios.
Improve debiasing performance on larger models with more intricate knowledge.
papers.abstract: Generating fair and accurate predictions plays a pivotal role in deploying large language models (LLMs) in the real world. However, existing debiasing methods inevitably generate unfair or incorrect predictions as they are designed and evaluated to achieve parity across different social groups but leave aside individual commonsense facts, resulting in modified knowledge that elicits unreasonable or undesired predictions. In this paper, we first establish a new bias mitigation benchmark, BiaScope, which systematically assesses performance by leveraging newly constructed datasets and metrics on knowledge retention and generalization. Then, we propose a novel debiasing approach, Fairness Stamp (FAST), which enables fine-grained calibration of individual social biases. FAST identifies the decisive layer responsible for storing social biases and then calibrates its outputs by integrating a small modular network, considering both bias mitigation and knowledge-preserving demands. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that FAST surpasses state-of-the-art baselines with superior debiasing performance while not compromising the overall model capability for knowledge retention and downstream predictions. This highlights the potential of fine-grained debiasing strategies to achieve fairness in LLMs.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the way knowledge is stored in MLP parameters and the performance of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Stronger large language models exhibit higher parameter specialization for knowledge storage in MLPs, and this specialization improves the efficiency of knowledge utilization and reduces hallucination.
papers.conclusion: Enhanced parameter specialization for knowledge storage correlates with superior performance in LLMs, and optimizing this specialization improves task performance and reduces hallucination, highlighting the importance of aligning knowledge storage with retrieval mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models show higher parameter specialization, with PSS correlating strongly with performance on knowledge tasks.
Parameter specialization increases with model scale within the same family.
Parameter specialization evolves during pretraining, increasing in later training steps.
Fine-tuning that enhances parameter specialization (FT-PV) improves performance on knowledge tasks and reduces hallucination compared to other fine-tuning strategies.
Specialized knowledge distribution helps compress knowledge and reduce interference from irrelevant information.
papers.limitation:
Only examined knowledge parameter specialization within the MLP, not attention modules.
Tested models only up to 14B parameters due to GPU limitations.
future_direction: Progressively narrow the focus to individual neurons to measure more precise Parameter Specialization.
Extend the concept to other model architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs).
papers.abstract: Over time, a growing wave of large language models from various series has been introduced to the community. Researchers are striving to maximize the performance of language models with constrained parameter sizes. However, from a microscopic perspective, there has been limited research on how to better store knowledge in model parameters, particularly within MLPs, to enable more effective utilization of this knowledge by the model. In this work, we analyze twenty publicly available open-source large language models to investigate the relationship between their strong performance and the way knowledge is stored in their corresponding MLP parameters. Our findings reveal that as language models become more advanced and demonstrate stronger knowledge capabilities, their parameters exhibit increased specialization. Specifically, parameters in the MLPs tend to be more focused on encoding similar types of knowledge. We experimentally validate that this specialized distribution of knowledge contributes to improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in these models. Furthermore, by conducting causal training experiments, we confirm that this specialized knowledge distribution plays a critical role in improving the model's efficiency in leveraging stored knowledge.

papers.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KNOWLEDGE EDITOR, a hyper-network-based method to edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning, while preserving other knowledge and ensuring consistency across paraphrases.
papers.conclusion: KNOWLEDGE EDITOR provides an effective and reliable method for editing factual knowledge in language models, meeting desiderata of generality, reliability, and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR achieves high success rate and retain accuracy on fact-checking and question answering tasks.
Using paraphrase supervision during training improves consistency across semantically equivalent inputs.
The updates predicted by KNOWLEDGE EDITOR are sparse and concentrated on attention weight matrices in lower layers, contrasting with gradient-based methods.
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR outperforms fine-tuning and constrained fine-tuning baselines in terms of retaining previous knowledge and generalization to paraphrases.
The hyper-network learns to project gradients to a different direction that preserves other knowledge while editing the target fact.
future_direction: Exploring multiple updates in a loop for editing.
Investigating the mechanism of knowledge encoding in LMs through the lens of editing.
papers.abstract: The factual knowledge acquired during pretraining and stored in the parameters of Language Models (LMs) can be useful in downstream tasks (e.g., question answering or textual inference). However, some facts can be incorrectly induced or become obsolete over time. We present KNOWLEDGEEDITOR, a method which can be used to edit this knowledge and, thus, fix 'bugs' or unexpected predictions without the need for expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Besides being computationally efficient, KNOWLEDGEEDITOR does not require any modifications in LM pretraining (e.g., the use of meta-learning). In our approach, we train a hyper-network with constrained optimization to modify a fact without affecting the rest of the knowledge; the trained hyper-network is then used to predict the weight update at test time. We show KNOWL-EDGEEDITOR's efficacy with two popular architectures and knowledge-intensive tasks: i) a BERT model fine-tuned for fact-checking, and ii) a sequence-to-sequence BART model for question answering. With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: Peer Review #3 of "Learning to perform role-filler binding with schematic knowledge (v0.2)"
papers.core_contribution: Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and DNC) can learn to perform role-filler binding without explicit labels and generalize to arbitrary fillers, even those that violate training correlations, by storing bindings in their external memory components.
papers.conclusion: Networks with external memory can learn role-filler binding, a key component for learning flexible, structured cognitive representations, by extracting relations from input structure rather than relying on training correlations.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with external memory (Fast Weights and DNC) learn to perform role-filler binding without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs.
These networks can generalize to previously unseen fillers when trained with an unlimited pool of fillers (Unlimited Filler Training).
The Fast Weights network shows biases towards statistical regularities from training, while the DNC does not, suggesting different binding mechanisms.
Decoding analyses indicate successful networks store role-filler bindings in their external memory components (fast weights matrix or memory buffer), not in the controller's hidden state.
Networks fail when test stories are presented in a radically different (shuffled) order from training, indicating reliance on structural similarities.
papers.limitation:
Networks fail when given stories presented in a radically different (shuffled) order from training.
The study does not prove that all standard RNN and LSTM models are unable to solve these tasks; future work with larger LSTMs might succeed.
future_direction: Training regimes that use shuffled stories during training to make models robust to test stories with shuffled segments.
Investigating how much a pool of train fillers needs to be expanded to allow networks to learn a representation that extends to previously unseen fillers.
Testing models of role-filler binding against neural data, potentially using paradigms for probing activity-silent memory.
papers.abstract: Through specific experiences, humans learn the relationships that underlie the structure of events in the world. Schema theory suggests that we organize this information in mental frameworks called "schemata," which represent our knowledge of the structure of the world. Generalizing knowledge of structural relationships to new situations requires rolefiller binding, the ability to associate specific "fillers" with abstract "roles." For instance, when we hear the sentence "Alice ordered a tea from Bob," the role-filler bindings "Alice:customer," "tea:drink," and "Bob:barista" allow us to understand and make inferences about the sentence. We can perform these bindings for arbitrary fillers -we understand this sentence even if we have never heard the names "Alice," "tea," or "Bob" before. In this work, we define a model as capable of performing role-filler binding if it can recall arbitrary fillers corresponding to a specified role, even when these pairings violate correlations seen during training. Previous work found that models can learn this ability when explicitly told what the roles and fillers are, or when given fillers seen during training. We show that networks with external memory learn to bind roles to arbitrary fillers, without explicitly labeled role-filler pairs. We further show that they can perform these bindings on role-filler pairs that violate correlations seen during training, while retaining knowledge of training correlations. We apply analyses inspired by neural decoding to interpret what the networks have learned.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and what are the different types of disagreement?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three classes of disagreement between LM outputs and internal probes—confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity—and shows that probes' superiority is often due to better calibration, and that ensembling probes and queries can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that mismatches between internal and external representations of truthfulness in LMs are diverse, primarily due to different prediction pathways rather than deceptive intent, and provides a taxonomy for understanding these disagreements.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries for evaluating truthfulness in language models.
Probes are better calibrated than queries, meaning their confidence scores more accurately reflect prediction correctness.
Most disagreements between queries and probes are due to confabulation (queries confident when probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), with deception being rare.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can further improve accuracy over using either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, indicating context-dependent behavior.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may affect the distribution of disagreements.
Presentation of only results on linear probes, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Future work may more systematically study the distribution of query–probe disagreements induced by different prompts.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs “lie’ or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today’s LMs, or can query–probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source
papers.research_question: How do LLMs prioritize between their learned parametric knowledge (PK) and external contextual knowledge (CK) when faced with conflicting information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing framework to study how LLMs select between parametric and contextual knowledge, showing that specific activations, especially from mid-layers and relation tokens, correlate with the knowledge source used.
papers.conclusion: Specific model activations correlate with knowledge source selection, and the probing framework generalizes across relation groups, enabling future work on controlling knowledge source behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Specific model activations are indicative of the knowledge source employed, with mid-layer activations, particularly those related to relations in the input, being crucial for prediction.
The most predictive features for knowledge source selection are those of the relation token in the query.
The knowledge source can be detected directly from the perturbing object token early in the inference process.
MHSA activations are less connected to the used knowledge source than MLP-L2 and MLP-L1 activations.
The probing framework successfully transfers learned knowledge source patterns from one relation group to another, demonstrating generalization.
papers.limitation:
The framework is designed to probe LLMs by introducing contradictions to their learned knowledge and does not account for situations where the knowledge remains unperturbed.
The study primarily measures correlation between activations and knowledge source use, but does not establish an explanation of the underlying process.
The framework uses a conventional subject-relation-object prompt structure, which may introduce biases; exploring alternative prompt structures could yield further insights.
future_direction: Extend the framework to handle cases where both parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge are consistent or not related.
Uncover the underlying mechanisms that govern knowledge source selection in LLMs through experimental designs that manipulate specific model parameters or activations.
Employ a variety of prompt structures to mitigate biases associated with the conventional subject-relation-object format.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often encounter conflicts between their learned, internal (parametric knowledge, PK) and external knowledge provided during inference (contextual knowledge, CK). Understanding how LLMs models prioritize one knowledge source over the other remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel probing framework to explore the mechanisms governing the selection between PK and CK in LLMs. Using controlled prompts designed to contradict the model's PK, we demonstrate that specific model activations are indicative of the knowledge source employed. We evaluate this framework on various LLMs of different sizes and demonstrate that mid-layer activations, particularly those related to relations in the input, are crucial in predicting knowledge source selection, paving the way for more reliable models capable of handling knowledge conflicts effectively.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: Deciphering the Interplay of Parametric and Non-parametric Memory in Retrieval-augmented Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the ATLAS model decide between using parametric (internal) and non-parametric (retrieved) memory, and which internal components are involved in copying from context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses causal mediation analysis to show that the ATLAS RAG model relies more on retrieved context than internal parametric knowledge when both are available, and identifies that MLP and Attention modules play distinct roles in copying and relevance evaluation.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that the ATLAS model performs a relevance evaluation using subject and relation tokens, then shifts focus to copy object tokens. The MLP in early to middle layers contextualizes relevance, while Attention in later layers integrates information for final answer extraction.
papers.key_findings:
The model tends to copy from the context (non-parametric memory) when the context is relevant.
Object tokens are the most impactful when the model is in copying mode.
The MLP in mid-layers is crucial for translating object token representations from the encoder to the decoder.
Subject and relation tokens are important for determining context relevance.
The MLP and Attention work together: MLP processes subject/relation tokens for relevance, and Attention integrates information for object extraction.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted on specific datasets (PopQA and PEQ), which may limit generalizability.
Using counterfactuals for context manipulation might not fully capture noisy or ambiguous real contexts.
Findings may not generalize to other RAG models, especially those not trained in a RAG setup.
The model may not handle outdated or rapidly changing information well.
future_direction: Generalizing the findings to other RAG models.
Studying model behavior in noisy or ambiguous contexts.
Investigating how models adjust to temporal changes in knowledge.
papers.abstract: Generative language models often struggle with specialized or less-discussed knowledge. A potential solution is found in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models which act like retrieving information before generating responses. In this study, we explore how the \textsc{Atlas} approach, a RAG model, decides between what it already knows (parametric) and what it retrieves (non-parametric). We use causal mediation analysis and controlled experiments to examine how internal representations influence information processing. Our findings disentangle the effects of parametric knowledge and the retrieved context. They indicate that in cases where the model can choose between both types of information (parametric and non-parametric), it relies more on the context than the parametric knowledge. Furthermore, the analysis investigates the computations involved in \emph{how} the model uses the information from the context. We find that multiple mechanisms are active within the model and can be detected with mediation analysis: first, the decision of \emph{whether the context is relevant}, and second, how the encoder computes output representations to support copying when relevant.

papers.title: AttnLRP: Attention-Aware Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we achieve faithful and computationally efficient attributions for the entire transformer model, including its latent representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AttnLRP, an extension of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) within the Deep Taylor Decomposition framework, to provide faithful and efficient attributions for transformer models, including their latent representations.
papers.conclusion: AttnLRP provides a faithful and efficient method for explaining transformer models, enabling both input and latent feature attribution, which opens the door for concept-based explanations.
papers.key_findings:
AttnLRP outperforms existing attribution methods in terms of faithfulness and computational efficiency.
AttnLRP enables the attribution and understanding of latent neurons (e.g., knowledge neurons in FFN layers).
The method successfully handles non-linear transformer components like softmax, matrix multiplication, and normalization layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models are prone to biased predictions and hallucinations, underlining the paramount importance of understanding their model-internal reasoning process. However, achieving faithful attributions for the entirety of a black-box transformer model and maintaining computational efficiency is an unsolved challenge. By extending the Layer-wise Relevance Propagation attribution method to handle attention layers, we address these challenges effectively. While partial solutions exist, our method is the first to faithfully and holistically attribute not only input but also latent representations of transformer models with the computational efficiency similar to a single backward pass. Through extensive evaluations against existing methods on LLaMa 2, Mixtral 8x7b, Flan-T5 and vision transformer architectures, we demonstrate that our proposed approach surpasses alternative methods in terms of faithfulness and enables the understanding of latent representations, opening up the door for concept-based explanations. We provide an LRP library at https://github.com/rachtibat/LRP-eXplains-Transformers.

papers.title: PERSONA: Dynamic and Compositional Inference-Time Personality Control via Activation Vector Algebra
papers.research_question: How can we achieve dynamic and compositional personality control in Large Language Models without fine-tuning, by directly manipulating personality vectors in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PERSONA, a training-free framework for dynamic and compositional personality control in LLMs via activation vector algebra, achieving fine-tuning level performance by extracting and manipulating orthogonal personality vectors in the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Personality control in LLMs can be achieved through activation vector algebra, providing evidence that aspects of LLM personality are mathematically tractable and opening new directions for interpretable and efficient behavioral control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits can be represented as approximately orthogonal, extractable vectors in the model's activation space via contrastive analysis.
These personality vectors support algebraic operations (scalar multiplication, addition, subtraction) for precise and compositional control of trait intensity and combination.
The PERSONA framework achieves a mean score of 9.60 on PersonalityBench, nearly matching the supervised fine-tuning upper bound of 9.61, and up to 91% win rates on the dynamic PERSONA-EVOLVE benchmark.
papers.abstract: Current methods for personality control in Large Language Models rely on static prompting or expensive fine-tuning, failing to capture the dynamic and compositional nature of human traits. We introduce PERSONA, a training-free framework that achieves fine-tuning level performance through direct manipulation of personality vectors in activation space. Our key insight is that personality traits appear as extractable, approximately orthogonal directions in the model's representation space that support algebraic operations. The framework operates through three stages: Persona-Base extracts orthogonal trait vectors via contrastive activation analysis; Persona-Algebra enables precise control through vector arithmetic (scalar multiplication for intensity, addition for composition, subtraction for suppression); and Persona-Flow achieves context-aware adaptation by dynamically composing these vectors during inference. On PersonalityBench, our approach achieves a mean score of 9.60, nearly matching the supervised fine-tuning upper bound of 9.61 without any gradient updates.
